final_proof:
Let us use the standard multiindex notation. Thus, for a multiindex \(\gamma=(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)\in\mathbb N_0^n\) and an \(n\)-tuple \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\), define
\[
 z^\gamma:=\prod_{j=1}^n z_j^{\gamma_j},
\]
where a zeroth power is interpreted as \(1\). Inequalities between multiindices are componentwise, and the multiindex binomial coefficient is
\[
 \binom{\alpha}{\beta}:=\prod_{j=1}^n \binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j}.
\]
Since addition of tuples is componentwise, the ordinary binomial theorem applied separately to every coordinate gives
\[
 (x+y)^\alpha
 =\prod_{j=1}^n (x_j+y_j)^{\alpha_j}
 =\prod_{j=1}^n\left(
     \sum_{k_j=0}^{\alpha_j}
       \binom{\alpha_j}{k_j}x_j^{k_j}y_j^{\alpha_j-k_j}
   \right).
\]
All sums and products here are finite. Therefore, repeated use of the distributive law expands the last product as
\[
 \sum_{(k_1,\ldots,k_n)\in\prod_{j=1}^n\{0,1,\ldots,\alpha_j\}}
 \prod_{j=1}^n\binom{\alpha_j}{k_j}x_j^{k_j}y_j^{\alpha_j-k_j}.
\]
The tuples \((k_1,\ldots,k_n)\) in this Cartesian product are precisely the multiindices \(\beta\) satisfying \(0\leq\beta\leq\alpha\). For such a \(\beta\), the corresponding summand is
\[
 \left(\prod_{j=1}^n\binom{\alpha_j}{\beta_j}\right)
 \left(\prod_{j=1}^n x_j^{\beta_j}\right)
 \left(\prod_{j=1}^n y_j^{\alpha_j-\beta_j}\right)
 =\binom{\alpha}{\beta}x^\beta y^{\alpha-\beta}.
\]
Substituting this expression into the preceding finite sum yields
\[
 (x+y)^\alpha=\sum_{0\leq\beta\leq\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}x^\beta y^{\alpha-\beta},
\]
as required.
